newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss offer central bank wider investment powers.
newsitem.headline: Swiss offer central bank wider investment powers.

text.p: Switzerland's central bank will be given more freedom to manage its investments in order to reap higher profits for public coffers under a proposed package of changes in its legal charter, the government said on Monday.
The government approved and passed to parliament a reform bill that would also reduce the gold reserve requirement of the Swiss National Bank (SNB) and allow it to carry out gold lending.

The bill, based on a report by SNB and finance ministry officials published last December, includes proposals to allow the central bank to use derivatives and invest in longer-dated and higher yielding debt by foreign states, banks or international organisations.
The report did not specify the type of derivative the central bank would be able to use.

"The Swiss National Bank should be able to achieve higher returns and pass along these profits to federal and cantonal (state) authorities," a government statement said about the purpose of the reforms.

The package is separate from a wider revision planned for 1998 that would revalue SNB reserves and use half of some 14 billion Swiss francs in added value to create a new humanitarian foundation, a plan unveiled by Berne on March 5.

Like most central banks, the SNB has a certain amount of gold in its vaults to back its currency. However, since the gold standard was scrapped in 1971, the SNB's gold reserves have not been used and are steady at around 2,600 tonnes.
The reform bill proposes the SNB be allowed to use gold lending facilities to improve the performance on gold reserves.

However, this could push the SNB below a mandated 40 percent reserve requirement for gold, a level the central bank is already close to breaching due to the ever-increasing amount of notes in circulation.
The bill therefore proposes cutting the reserve requirement for gold to 25 percent from 40 percent of notes in circulation.
The package would also abolish federal taxes on the SNB because such taxes only serve to reduce the amount of money it can transfer.

The proposals for a partial revision of the national bank law would boost SNB annual income by an estimated 400 million Swiss francs and thus also raise the amount of money it transfers to federal and cantonal governments.
The proposals stem from a working group created in June last year to look for ways to improve SNB investment policy after criticism prompted by a drop in its annual payment to public coffers.

Between 1991 and 1994 the SNB transferred around 605 million Swiss francs annually to federal and cantonal Swiss governments, but this plunged to 147 million Swiss francs in 1995 due to the fall in the dollar and yen, which necessitated higher write-offs on currency reserves.
